extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, designers, and critics interested in architectural beauty and ornament (esp. Gothic/Venetian traditions)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidelines for designing and evaluating architectural beauty: massing, treatment of light and shadow, ornamentation, and the appropriate imitation of natural forms, with examples drawn from Gothic, Venetian, Greek, Lombard and Tudor work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of mass and breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: “the relative majesty of buildings depends more on the weight and vigor of their masses than on any other attribute of their design: mass of everything, of bulk, of light, of darkness, of color... breadth of them; not broken light, nor scattered darkness, nor divided weight, but solid stone, broad sunshine, starless shade.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for broad, solid masses rather than intricate small detail. Achieve power by weight, solidity and large areas of light and shadow (e.g., penthouse roofs producing grand masses of shadow, sloping roofs, jutting porches, projecting balconies, hollow niches, massy gargoyles, frowning parapets). Avoid small, cramped, neat, or excessively precise detailing that reduces perceived size and vigor. Practical advice: prioritize 'gloom and simplicity' to obtain majesty; ordinary builders can achieve vigor by bold massing even if incapable of fine carving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of light and darkness: gradation, flatness, and breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: “the principal circumstances traceable in the treatment of the two kinds of masses of light and darkness... gradation in the one, flatness in the other, and breadth in both, being the qualities sought and exhibited.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage light- and dark-masses deliberately: use gradation where appropriate and flat, broad dark areas elsewhere; ensure both are broad to create a balanced composition. Avoid scattered or broken light and thin, divided shadows. This principle governs tracery and moulding design and was central to earlier architects’ methods before hue was used as the main division of surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in imitation of natural forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'peculiar restraint in the imitation of natural forms' constitutes the dignity of luxuriant work; beauty often arises from restrained imitation rather than slavish copying of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using natural motifs, exercise restraint: don't merely reproduce nature in a clumsy or excessive way. The dignity of ornament comes from controlled adaptation of natural forms — subtle undercutting, measured stylization, and avoiding overabundance that turns vitality into chaos. Reserve full luxuriant imitation for where the craft and judgment to manage it exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must derive from common natural forms (Frequency → Beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms not taken from natural objects tend to be ugly: 'I would assume... that forms which are not taken from natural objects must be ugly' and that frequency in nature is a test of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor ornament and forms that echo frequently seen, familiar natural shapes (trees, leaves, pebbles, spirals). Use the 'frequency to beauty' test: forms common in everyday nature are likelier to be perceived as beautiful. Avoid invented motifs that have no natural precedent or visible frequency, since they risk being perceived as 'monstrous' or ugly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer curves and natural lines over straight lines when seeking beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “all most lovely forms and thoughts are directly taken from natural objects... all perfectly beautiful forms must be composed of curves; since there is hardly any common natural form in which it is possible to discover a straight line.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curves as primary elements of beauty; introduce straight lines only when structurally necessary and when their arrangement corresponds to natural groupings of straight forms (e.g., crystalline or geological forms). Where straight lines are required, fit them into patterns defensible by natural precedents (as in Lombard ornament which echoes common crystal forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep mouldings and cusps simple and flat to preserve purity of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier Venetian mouldings kept cusps perfectly flat, decorated only minimally (trefoil or fillet 'just traceable and no more'), so that quatrefoil and cusps read clearly even from a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dense flower-work or ornamental knots that interfere with the purity and legibility of mouldings. Keep cusps sharp or only slightly truncated; if decorated, do so sparingly (a simple trefoil or fillet). Set glazing back behind stone-work so that glass does not produce distracting reflections and the stone's depth reads clearly (examples: Palazzo Foscari, Doge's Palace). Corrupted or over-decorated forms (Casa d'Oro, Palazzo Pisani) show the loss of design majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Greek guilloche (fret) and other non‑natural frets as surface decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek fret (guilloche) is accused of being 'ugly' or 'monstrous' because its precedent is an artificial crystal of bismuth — rare and unnatural; the author prefers an uncarved fillet or plinth to one covered with this concatenation of straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use repetitive geometric frets that lack common natural analogues as primary ornament; they jar with the eye unless used extremely small (coins) or as a foil to true ornament. Prefer simpler, plainer mouldings where such frets would otherwise be customary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn Tudor portcullis/reticulation as unsuitable small-surface ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tudor portcullis (reticulation) is criticised: though reticulation exists in nature, the portcullis pattern—especially when diminished and set on a solid surface—is 'absolutely and unmitigatedly frightful'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using dense reticulated patterns (portcullis) as small surface ornament; if reticulation is used, it should reflect naturally varied meshes and sizes and allow shade through bars. Small, rigid rete patterns on solid surfaces are awkward and demeaning to the stone-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heraldic decoration sparingly and as inscriptionary, not as repeated ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Heraldic decoration has pride and significance and belongs in prominent places (over gates) or where its legend can be read, but repeated heraldry as all-over ornament 'will utterly destroy both the power and beauty of any building.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve coats of arms and similar devices for a few appropriate locations. If repeating a symbol, choose a single, fair emblem (fleur-de-lis, giglio bianco, English rose) rather than multiplying complex armorial bearings. Treat heraldry primarily as identity/information, not as patterning ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters and inscriptions should be functional and legible — not ornamental
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are especially unlike nature and are 'frightful things' as ornament; they should be endured only where their intellectual office matters — 'Place them where they will be read, and there only; and let them be plainly written.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use lettering as decorative surface pattern. Put inscriptions in locations where people can read them; write simply and plainly; avoid overly ornate letterforms, upside-down placements, or tricky arrangements that make the inscription illegible. Inscriptions are interruptions for sense, not visual ornament — treat them as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use flying ribands/scrolls as ornament; prefer tablets for text
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribands or flying scrolls lack natural structure (no skeleton, no beginning or end) and spoil nearby forms; tablets are honest, rational supports for writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flourished scrolls and ribands as surface ornament. If text is required, present it on a plain tablet or roll designed to be functional, not as an ornamental flourish. Let flowers hang loose rather than be artificially tied with ribbon motifs that have no natural analogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery is not a noble sculptural subject by itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery 'as such, is always ignoble; it becomes a subject of interest only by the colors it bears and the contexts it supports.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make drapery the principal sculptural motif or treat it as standalone ornament; when used, ensure it has a clear structural and chromatic purpose and does not become an aimless decorative mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve broad surfaces in mouldings and avoid small ridgy fillets that break gradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mouldings of early times were composed of alternate square and cylindrical shafts so the eye dwelt on broad surfaces; later, a ridgy fillet appears on the outer edge and grows, at first sharp then truncated into a definite fillet, eventually subordinating the roll to the fillet and destroying broad gradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor moulding profiles where the eye rests on broad surfaces and clear gradations of light; resist the growth of minute fillets and ridges that multiply sharp lines of light and fragment the effect. Let mouldings keep clear concavities edged by delicate fillets upon which the eye rests, rather than cluttered fine projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set glazing behind stonework to maintain depth and avoid glare
rubrics_metrics.description: “the glass of the window, where there was any, was... thrown back behind the stone-work, that no flashes of light might interfere with its depth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recess glazing so that reflections or flashes do not flatten or distract from the carved stone tracery; ensure the stone's depth and shadow read clearly from a distance (example: Palazzo Foscari, Doge's Palace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical route to power: use simple devices to make weight and shadow
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It matters not how clumsy, how common, the means are, that get weight and shadow... get but gloom and simplicity, and all good things will follow in their place and time.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fine composition or carving is unavailable, attain architectural power through simple, robust devices: large sloping roofs, projecting balconies, deep porches, hollow niches, large shadow-casting elements and warm textured surfaces (moss, lichen). Designers should first secure solidity ('owl's eyes') and later refine detail ('falcon's').
